REASONS AND JUDGMENT
I. Overview [1] The Applicant, Hong Zhang, challenges a decision re-determining her eligibility for the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB), which she received for the period from March 15, 2020, to February 26, 2022. She claims that she was denied procedural fairness because she was not made aware of the concerns regarding the information she submitted. She also challenges the reasonableness of the decision because information which she submitted was not considered.

[2] For the reasons below, procedural fairness was breached because the Second Reviewer relied upon contacting Ms. Zhang by telephone, a method of contact that had previously failed, without attempting to contact her by mail, which was a contact method that was successful in reaching Ms. Zhang. The application for judicial review is therefore granted.
II. Background [3] Ms. Zhang received benefits for CERB and the Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB) from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). The present application challenges only the determination that she was ineligible for the CERB benefits she received.

[4] In a letter from CRA dated June 17, 2024, Ms. Zhang was advised that she needed to submit additional information to confirm her eligibility for the programs within 45 days. In response to the letter, on July 23, 2024, she uploaded a number of documents, including receipts, handwritten notes, bank statements, email exchanges, and document packages. These documents were written in both English and Mandarin, with a majority of the documents in Mandarin.

[5] A CRA First Reviewer called Ms. Zhang on October 29 and October 30, 2024, to discuss the uploaded documents. There was no response to the first call and no capacity to leave a message on Ms. Zhang’s voicemail. There was also no response to the second call, but a voicemail was left requesting Ms. Zhang to contact the First Reviewer before the end of the day on November 2, 2024. No return call was received by the CRA.

[6] On November 5, 2024, the CRA determined Ms. Zhang to be ineligible for the benefits she received because she did not establish that she earned less than $1000 during the eligibility period, nor did she establish that she stopped working or had reduced hours for reasons related to COVID-19. The First Reviewer noted that much of the information submitted by Ms. Zhang was not in English or French.

[7] Ms. Zhang disagreed with the CRA’s determination, and a Second Review was commenced.

[8] The Second Reviewer called Ms. Zhang on August 21, 2025, and called her twice on August 25, 2025, using the same telephone number used by the First Reviewer. There was no response to these calls and no capacity to leave a voicemail message.

subthemes.text:
[19] Before determining whether Ms. Zhang’s right to procedural fairness was breached, the level of procedural fairness owed to Ms. Zhang must be determined. The level of procedural fairness owed in a specific context is “eminently variable” and its content is determined by examining the decision-making context in each case (Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 CanLII 699 (SCC), [1999] 2 SCR 817 [Baker] at para 21).

[20] The present context involves a second-level review of a decision re-determining Ms. Zhang’s eligibility for the benefits she received. The level of fairness owed in this context may be determined by applying the contextual factors identified by the Supreme Court of Canada in Baker. The following factors determining participatory rights were identified (Baker at paras 23-27):
the nature of the decision being made and the process followed in making it: essentially, the closer the nature of the decision and the process is to a judicial model, the higher the procedural protections;
the nature of the statutory scheme and the “terms of the statute pursuant to which the body operates”: the role of the decision being made in the context of the statute, and avenues for recourse are relevant considerations within this factor;
the importance of the decision to the individual or individuals affected: “The more important the decision is to the lives of those affected and the greater its impact on that person or those persons, the more stringent the procedural protections that will be mandated”;
the legitimate expectations of the person challenging the decision: if a person has been legitimately led to believe that a certain process or result will ensue, greater procedural protections will be applied; and
the choices of procedure made by the agency itself: appropriate deference should be given to the expertise as well as institutional constraints of an agency in exercising their choice of procedures when they are given that choice.

[21] Applying these factors to the second-level review of the determination of Ms. Zhang’s ineligibility for her benefits, I find that a moderate level of procedural fairness was owed in the process of re-determining Ms. Zhang’s eligibility for the benefits she received.

[22] Regarding the first factor, the second-level review of an eligibility re-determination is administrative in nature, and the process does not have any features of judicial decision-making. There is no right to counsel, and information is collected and assessed informally, through written and telephone communications of indefinite duration. This factor indicates more relaxed procedural fairness standards.

[23] The determinative nature of an eligibility re-determination decision is a relevant consideration regarding the second factor. The statutory scheme does not provide a statutory appeal mechanism (Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act, SC 2020, c 5, s 8), although judicial review may be sought in the Federal Court, with a presumptive deferential standard of review applied to the decision. The determinative nature of the decision militates in favour of a moderate level of fairness.

[24] Regarding the third Baker factor, a decision to re-determine eligibility for financial benefits which a person has already received has a moderate to high level of importance for the individual. Such a determination is distinct from a determination of initial eligibility prior to payment and receipt of benefits because the chances are higher that benefit recipients have conducted themselves based on benefit entitlement, disposing of the benefits for their financial support. The consequences of repayment of the benefits lands more harshly on recipients in these circumstances given their expectation of entitlement, which rises in proportion to the time that elapses between benefit payment and the re-determination of eligibility. This factor indicates that a moderate to high level of fairness is warranted.

[25] The fourth factor examines legitimate expectations, and while Ms. Zhang was never assured that more than one method of contact would be used to reach her, in practice she received communication from the CRA both by mail and by telephone. It follows that she would have legitimately expected the CRA to contact her using an alternative method if there was a history of failure in contacting her using one of the two communication methods. This factor points toward a moderate level of fairness.

[26] On the fifth and final factor, the choice of the CRA’s procedures and institutional constraints also indicates that a moderate level of fairness was owed. Despite a lack of obligation in statute or policy to communicate using alternate methods, the CRA chose to do so in some of its communications with Ms. Zhang. This indicates that institutional considerations such as lack of resources, inefficiency or urgency in the eligibility re-determination did not constrain the agency from using more than one method of communication.

[27] I am aware that previous decisions of this Court have placed general procedural fairness obligations owed by the CRA at the low end of the spectrum (Ramanathan v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FC 1029 at para 46; Cozak v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FC 1571 at para 17; Baidar v Canada (Attorney General), 2025 FC 431 at para 34). However, the analysis is contextual and the contextual factors from Baker indicate that a moderate level of procedural fairness was owed to Ms. Zhang in the second-level re-determination of her eligibility for the benefits she received.

subthemes.text:
[28] The application of a moderate level of procedural fairness to Ms. Zhang’s circumstances reveals that procedural fairness was breached. The Second Reviewer knew or should have known the history of failed telephone communications with Ms. Zhang, and the success in communicating with Ms. Zhang by mail. It was unfair for the Second Reviewer to persist in attempts to communicate with Ms. Zhang using a previously unsuccessful method when an effective alternative was available. By doing so, the Second Reviewer deprived Ms. Zhang of her participatory rights, including her right to know the concerns she had to meet.
V. Conclusion [29] The moderate level of procedural fairness applicable to the second-level review of Ms. Zhang’s ineligibility for benefits reveals that procedural fairness was breached by the Officer’s persistence in only using communication methods known to have previously failed. As a result, the application for judicial review is granted, and it is unnecessary to assess the reasonableness of the decision.
JUDGMENT in T-3772-25
THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that:
The style of cause is amended to reflect the Attorney General of Canada as the proper Respondent, effective immediately.
The Application for Judicial Review is granted, the determination of the Applicant’s ineligibility for benefits is set aside, and the matter is remitted to a different Officer for redetermination in a manner consistent with these reasons.
There is no order regarding cost.

PRESENT: The Honourable Justice Battista
BETWEEN:
HONG ZHANG
Applicant
and
THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF CANADA

REASONS AND JUDGMENT
I. Overview [1] The Applicant, Hong Zhang, challenges a decision re-determining her eligibility for the Canada Emergency Response Benefit (CERB), which she received for the period from March 15, 2020, to February 26, 2022. She claims that she was denied procedural fairness because she was not made aware of the concerns regarding the information she submitted. She also challenges the reasonableness of the decision because information which she submitted was not considered.

[2] For the reasons below, procedural fairness was breached because the Second Reviewer relied upon contacting Ms. Zhang by telephone, a method of contact that had previously failed, without attempting to contact her by mail, which was a contact method that was successful in reaching Ms. Zhang. The application for judicial review is therefore granted.
II. Background [3] Ms. Zhang received benefits for CERB and the Canada Recovery Sickness Benefit (CRSB) from the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). The present application challenges only the determination that she was ineligible for the CERB benefits she received.

[4] In a letter from CRA dated June 17, 2024, Ms. Zhang was advised that she needed to submit additional information to confirm her eligibility for the programs within 45 days. In response to the letter, on July 23, 2024, she uploaded a number of documents, including receipts, handwritten notes, bank statements, email exchanges, and document packages. These documents were written in both English and Mandarin, with a majority of the documents in Mandarin.

[5] A CRA First Reviewer called Ms. Zhang on October 29 and October 30, 2024, to discuss the uploaded documents. There was no response to the first call and no capacity to leave a message on Ms. Zhang’s voicemail. There was also no response to the second call, but a voicemail was left requesting Ms. Zhang to contact the First Reviewer before the end of the day on November 2, 2024. No return call was received by the CRA.

[6] On November 5, 2024, the CRA determined Ms. Zhang to be ineligible for the benefits she received because she did not establish that she earned less than $1000 during the eligibility period, nor did she establish that she stopped working or had reduced hours for reasons related to COVID-19. The First Reviewer noted that much of the information submitted by Ms. Zhang was not in English or French.
[7] Ms. Zhang disagreed with the CRA’s determination, and a Second Review was commenced.

[8] The Second Reviewer called Ms. Zhang on August 21, 2025, and called her twice on August 25, 2025, using the same telephone number used by the First Reviewer. There was no response to these calls and no capacity to leave a voicemail message.

[9] The Second Reviewer noted that the information supplied by Ms. Zhang was insufficient to determine her eligibility for the benefits she received, and noted the need for documentation such as paystubs, bank statements, records of employment, invoices, bank statements and any documents that Ms. Zhang believed is relevant to her eligibility for COVID benefits. Ms. Zhang was therefore deemed ineligible for the benefits she received.
III. Issues and Standards of Review [10] The Respondent requests that the Attorney General of Canada be identified as the proper Respondent in this matter, given the responsibility of the Attorney General of Canada for decisions regarding eligibility for CERB benefits. Ms. Zhang consented to this change. The style of cause will therefore be amended pursuant to the Respondent’s request, effective immediately.

[11] The Respondent objects to the admissibility of evidence contained in the Application Record which was not before the decision maker. No standard of review is required for the resolution of this issue, which is resolved by applying the principles regarding the admissibility of new evidence on judicial review (Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada v Canadian Copyright Licensing Agency (Access Copyright), 2012 FCA 22 [Access Copyright] at para 20).

[12] The issues of procedural fairness raised by Ms. Zhang require the Court to ask whether the procedure followed by the decision-maker was fair and just having regard to all the circumstances (Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54).
[13] The reasonableness of the decision is evaluated pursuant to the reasonableness standard described in Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65.

IV. Analysis A. The new information presented by Ms. Zhang will be disregarded [14] The Respondent has requested that the Court disregard Exhibits C, D and E attached to Ms. Zhang’s Affidavit in her Application Record because they were not before the decision maker.

[15] In fact, none of these materials appear in the Certified Tribunal Record, which is presumed to be complete (Khan v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2025 FC 1282 at para 17). Ms. Zhang does not provide details regarding when and how these materials were submitted.

[16] The Court may only admit new evidence on judicial review in three circumstances: i) to provide general background information; ii) to highlight procedural fairness defects; and iii) to demonstrate the complete absence of evidence in the record on a particular finding (Access Copyright at para 20). The new evidence submitted by Ms. Zhang does not correspond to any of these circumstances and will be disregarded.
B. Procedural fairness was breached by the Second Reviewer’s failure to make sufficient attempts to contact Ms. Zhang [17] Ms. Zhang does not contest that the CRA tried to contact her using the telephone number she provided on five occasions, and that she was unresponsive. Ms. Zhang explains that she experienced telephone service issues, and also that she did not respond to the calls because she did not recognize the Vancouver number that called her.

[18] Ms. Zhang states that she was denied procedural fairness because the CRA did not make sufficient attempts to contact her. She argues that she provided both her mailing address as well as her telephone number, and when one method of contact failed the alternative method should have been attempted.

[19] Before determining whether Ms. Zhang’s right to procedural fairness was breached, the level of procedural fairness owed to Ms. Zhang must be determined. The level of procedural fairness owed in a specific context is “eminently variable” and its content is determined by examining the decision-making context in each case (Baker v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 1999 CanLII 699 (SCC), [1999] 2 SCR 817 [Baker] at para 21).

[21] Applying these factors to the second-level review of the determination of Ms. Zhang’s ineligibility for her benefits, I find that a moderate level of procedural fairness was owed in the process of re-determining Ms. Zhang’s eligibility for the benefits she received.

[22] Regarding the first factor, the second-level review of an eligibility re-determination is administrative in nature, and the process does not have any features of judicial decision-making. There is no right to counsel, and information is collected and assessed informally, through written and telephone communications of indefinite duration. This factor indicates more relaxed procedural fairness standards.

[23] The determinative nature of an eligibility re-determination decision is a relevant consideration regarding the second factor. The statutory scheme does not provide a statutory appeal mechanism (Canada Emergency Response Benefit Act, SC 2020, c 5, s 8), although judicial review may be sought in the Federal Court, with a presumptive deferential standard of review applied to the decision. The determinative nature of the decision militates in favour of a moderate level of fairness.

[24] Regarding the third Baker factor, a decision to re-determine eligibility for financial benefits which a person has already received has a moderate to high level of importance for the individual. Such a determination is distinct from a determination of initial eligibility prior to payment and receipt of benefits because the chances are higher that benefit recipients have conducted themselves based on benefit entitlement, disposing of the benefits for their financial support. The consequences of repayment of the benefits lands more harshly on recipients in these circumstances given their expectation of entitlement, which rises in proportion to the time that elapses between benefit payment and the re-determination of eligibility. This factor indicates that a moderate to high level of fairness is warranted.

[25] The fourth factor examines legitimate expectations, and while Ms. Zhang was never assured that more than one method of contact would be used to reach her, in practice she received communication from the CRA both by mail and by telephone. It follows that she would have legitimately expected the CRA to contact her using an alternative method if there was a history of failure in contacting her using one of the two communication methods. This factor points toward a moderate level of fairness.

[26] On the fifth and final factor, the choice of the CRA’s procedures and institutional constraints also indicates that a moderate level of fairness was owed. Despite a lack of obligation in statute or policy to communicate using alternate methods, the CRA chose to do so in some of its communications with Ms. Zhang. This indicates that institutional considerations such as lack of resources, inefficiency or urgency in the eligibility re-determination did not constrain the agency from using more than one method of communication.

[27] I am aware that previous decisions of this Court have placed general procedural fairness obligations owed by the CRA at the low end of the spectrum (Ramanathan v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FC 1029 at para 46; Cozak v Canada (Attorney General), 2023 FC 1571 at para 17; Baidar v Canada (Attorney General), 2025 FC 431 at para 34). However, the analysis is contextual and the contextual factors from Baker indicate that a moderate level of procedural fairness was owed to Ms. Zhang in the second-level re-determination of her eligibility for the benefits she received.

[28] The application of a moderate level of procedural fairness to Ms. Zhang’s circumstances reveals that procedural fairness was breached. The Second Reviewer knew or should have known the history of failed telephone communications with Ms. Zhang, and the success in communicating with Ms. Zhang by mail. It was unfair for the Second Reviewer to persist in attempts to communicate with Ms. Zhang using a previously unsuccessful method when an effective alternative was available. By doing so, the Second Reviewer deprived Ms. Zhang of her participatory rights, including her right to know the concerns she had to meet.
V. Conclusion [29] The moderate level of procedural fairness applicable to the second-level review of Ms. Zhang’s ineligibility for benefits reveals that procedural fairness was breached by the Officer’s persistence in only using communication methods known to have previously failed. As a result, the application for judicial review is granted, and it is unnecessary to assess the reasonableness of the decision.
JUDGMENT in T-3772-25
THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that:
The style of cause is amended to reflect the Attorney General of Canada as the proper Respondent, effective immediately.
The Application for Judicial Review is granted, the determination of the Applicant’s ineligibility for benefits is set aside, and the matter is remitted to a different Officer for redetermination in a manner consistent with these reasons.
There is no order regarding cost.
“Michael Battista”
Judge
